newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Valley warns California on ballot issue.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Valley warns California on ballot issue.

text.p: California's high technology industry is gearing up for a heavy assault against a securities litigation ballot initiative it says will cost jobs and cause companies to quit the state.

On Thursday, the American Electronics Association released a survey which found that 47 percent of public high technology companies among it members would consider leaving the state if the state's Proposition 211 ballot initiative passes.

Proposition 211, which expands a California initiative that failed in the primary season, is being promoted as a measure to protect investors from securities fraud and spectacles such as the 1980s banking and loan debacle.

The measure would make corporate executives and directors personally liable for losses and for civil damages in shareholder lawsuits over statements, or omission of statements, regarding material facts related to companies.

But California's booming high-tech industry, concentrated in Silicon Valley just south of San Francisco, argue that the measure's real beneficiaries would be securities lawyers filing lawsuits which are now sharply limited under a 1995 securities law.

Taxpayers Against Frivolous Lawsuits, a high tech alliance of corporations and investors spearheaded by prominent Kleiner Perkins Caufield and Byers venture capital partner John Doerr, claims the measure could cost companies billions of dollars.
The organisation plans to increase it spending on advertisements against the proposal by four-fold from this week until the Nov. 5 ballot.
Recent polling data commissioned by the anti-211 group found 25 percent of Californians surveyed favoured and 30 percent opposed the measure, but a huge 45 percent of voters were undecided.

The group, which is rallying Silicon Valley executives for what many claim is their first high profile political battle, cites economist estimates the proposition could cost over 150,000 jobs and cost businesses $1.3 billion a year.
It argues many companies, to avoid distracting legal tangles, would be forced to settle rather than fight costly court battles even in cases they regard as without merit.

Furthermore, the opponents argue, greater personal liability for company directors would discourage business talent from holding board positions -- Doerr has said Kleiner partners would resign directorships on public companies.

"Who will want to be an officer of a public company? Who will want to be a director of a public company?" asked Roger McNamee, a founding partner of Kleiner's Integral Capital Partners investment affiliate, in a luncheon presentation to professional investors this week.

In early August, both President Clinton and Republican Presidential candidate Bob Dole came out against the measure and Silicon Valley executives on both sides site the threat of 211 as the reason for supporting their candidate.

The AEA survey of 320 public member companies in California, carried out in August, found that 48 percent of respondents believed frivolous lawsuits or the threat of such lawsuits hindered their growth and made them less competitive.
These companies currently employ more than 61,000, or 7 percent of the nearly 900,000 high technology jobs that the AEA estimates are currently held in Californa.
Fifty-four percent of the companies polled believe frivolous lawsuits play a large part in their everyday business decisions, according to the survey.

Also, 96 to 98 percent of companies surveyed currently indemnify their officers and directors to protect them and their families from personal financial ruin as a result of shareholder lawsuits, which would be barred by Prop 211.

"The potential damage from Prop 211 goes way beyond California," Thom Weisel, chairman and chief executive of Montgomery Securities said in a document distributed at the firm's investor conference here. "Any public company with one single California shareholder is vulnerable."
